newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: New Zealand set to swing left in landmark election.
newsitem.headline: New Zealand set to swing left in landmark election.

text.p: New Zealand looked poised to swing to the left after six years of conservative government as early results flowed in from Saturday's general election.
Projections by TV3 network with 37 percent of the vote counted said the governing National Party was set to remain the largest in parliament, with about 44 of the 120 seats.
A potential National ally, the radical free-market Act New Zealand, was on track to win seven seats and the small centrist United party was expected to win one.
But the main opposition Labour Party, nationalist New Zealand First and left-wing Alliance were on course to win about 68 seats and could oust National if they can form a coalition.
"I'm very optimistic at this stage. I think things are looking very good for us," said Labour Party President Michael Hirschfeld.

"We're exceeding our expectations. The National Party are clearly falling a long way behind theirs...We are clearly going to be the dominant party other than National and that is going to put us in a position in a strong way to form a government," he told Radio New Zealand.
Before the poll, most commentators saw a left-wing coalition as the likeliest outcome, but New Zealand First's Maori leader Winston Peters has not ruled out a deal to keep National in power.
"Where Peters goes, I guess, goes government," said government spokesman Richard Griffin.
Turnout was very high, around 90 percent, in New Zealand's first election under a new proportional system which will favour minority or coalition governments.
National, under Prime Minister Jim Bolger, campaigned on its record of strong economic growth and tax cuts but opinion polls showed it rapidly losing support to Labour in recent weeks.

Labour, whose leader Helen Clark is bidding to become the country's first woman prime minister, promised to share more widely the fruits of economic recovery and pour extra funds into health, education and welfare.
Voters had a choice of 21 parties ranging from the Natural Law Party advocating yogic flying to the pro-marijuana Aotearoa Legalise Cannabis Party and the joke McGillicuddy Serious Party.
Unlike under the former first-past-the-post system, a clear decision on who rules may not be known for weeks. A government will only be agreed after complex negotiations.
New Zealand First, widely seen as playing the role of kingmaker, has campaigned for more open and accountable government and limits on foreign ownership, particularly of "strategic" assets.
The left-wing Alliance, which wants big increases in taxes and government spending, has ruled out joining a coalition but hinted it may support Labour on key issues.
